passages.original: Possunt ct ipsum Dominum, qui ejusdem continentiæ donum commendans ait, Sunt qui seipsos castraverunt propter regnum cælorum (Matth. xix, 12). Legunt quippe isti litteriones : sic enim potius quam litterati appellandi sunt qui legendo litterates, nihil saprre didicerunt : legunt ergo apud Ciceronem tale aliquid, unic sibi, videantur docte Christi verba culpare, perditi potius quam periti. Ille namque cum doceret, in trenslatione verborum obscœnitatem esse vitandam, Nolo, inquit, dici, morte Africani castratam esse rempublicam (Cic , de Oratore, lib. 3). Sed si hoc verbum ipse quod vitari volebat, ul vitandum ostenderet, non vitavit, ct quod dici noluit, coactus est dicere; quanto magis rcs quæ verbo eodem recte significatur, ut ab audiente possit intelligi, suo verbo enuntiatur?
passages.english: They can [find fault with] the Lord himself too, who, commending the gift of this same continence, says: "There are those who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven" (Matt. 19:12). For these letter-mongers read (for that is what they should be called rather than lettered men, since in reading letters they have learned to understand nothing), they read, then, something of this kind in Cicero, by which they may seem to themselves to find learned fault with the words of Christ, being depraved rather than skilled. For when he was teaching that obscenity is to be avoided in the metaphorical use of words, he said: "I do not want it said that by the death of Africanus the republic was castrated" (Cicero, On the Orator, book 3). But if he himself did not avoid this very word which he wished to be avoided, in order to show that it was to be avoided, and was compelled to say what he did not want said, how much more is a thing that is rightly signified by that same word expressed by its own word, so that it can be understood by the hearer?
passages.notes: The first sentence lacks a verb of censure; "reprehendi" is understood from the preceding context ("potest a verbosis impiis reprehendi et apostolus Paulus"), so read "they can [censure] the Lord himself". "Litteriones" is a contemptuous coinage, set against "litterati". Scanning errors corrected silently: ct/et, saprre/sapere, unic/unde, trenslatione/translatione, ul/ut, rcs/res.
